question: Why is a positive test for a rare disease usually a false alarm?

scene.title: Why is a positive test for a rare disease usually a false alarm?
scene.subtitle: A test that is right 99 times in 100 says you have a disease that 1 person in 1,000 has. The chance that you do is about 1 in 11.
scene.why: Medical tests, spam filters and fraud alerts all face this: when what you look for is rarer than a test’s false alarms, most alarms are false.
scene.opening: A test that is right 99 times in 100 says you have a rare disease. How likely is it that you really do?

beats.title: A thousand people
beats.body: Picture 1,000 people taking a test for a disease that 1 person in 1,000 has. The test is right 99 times in 100, for sick and healthy alike, so a positive feels 99% certain.

beats.title: Who tests positive
beats.body: The test finds the one sick person. But it also wrongly flags 1 healthy person in 100, which is about 10 of the 999.

beats.title: 1 in 11
beats.body: Gather everyone who tested positive: 11 people, and only 1 of them is sick. So a positive means about a 1 in 11 chance, not 99 in 100. That is still about 90 times the 1 in 1,000 before the test.

beats.title: Why it happens
beats.body: The false alarms come from the 999 healthy people, a group far bigger than the sick. If 1 in 100 were sick, as common as the false alarms, the sick would match them: even odds.

scene.takeaway: When a disease is rarer than a test’s false alarms, most positives are healthy people wrongly flagged, so doctors check them with a different test.

questions.q: A disease affects 1 person in 10, and the test is right 99 times in 100. Is a positive result still usually a false alarm?
questions.a: No. Of 1,000 people, about 100 are sick and 99 of them test positive, while about 9 of the 900 healthy are false alarms. A positive is right about 92% of the time.

questions.q: Why does a second, independent test help so much?
questions.a: Of 10,000 people, about 10 sick people test positive twice, while only about 1 of the 100 false alarms repeats. So two positives are right about 10 times in 11. A different kind of test helps most, because repeating the same test can repeat the same mistake.

questions.q: Does this mean the test is bad?
questions.a: No. It is right for about 990 of every 1,000 people. But this disease is rarer than the test’s false alarms, so those few false alarms still outnumber the sick.
